l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: Isaiah the son of Amoz is identified as the one who saw the vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem. His vision dates to the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD calls heaven and earth to hear, says he nourished and raised children who rebelled, and rejects the people's sacrifices, feasts, and prayers. He commands them to wash, cease evil, and seek justice, offers to make their sins white as snow if they are willing and obedient, and threatens the sword if they refuse. He declares he will turn his hand on the city, purge its dross, restore its judges and counselors, and consume those who forsake him.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: Israel is portrayed as a rebellious child that does not know or consider its owner, unlike the ox and donkey. It is called a sinful nation loaded with iniquity, wounded from foot to head, with its country desolate and cities burned. Only a very small remnant left by the LORD of Armies keeps it from being like Sodom and Gomorrah.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: The daughter of Zion is described as left like a shelter in a vineyard, a hut in a melon field, and a besieged city. The LORD promises that Zion shall be redeemed with justice and her converts with righteousness.

l: sacrifices and offerings, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD says he has had enough of burnt offerings of rams, fat of fed animals, and the blood of bulls, lambs, and male goats. He calls vain offerings, incense, New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations an abomination and a burden because they accompany evil and hands full of blood.

l: sin and judgment, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: The people are called loaded with iniquity, and their sins are said to be like scarlet and crimson, though the LORD offers to make them white as snow and wool. Refusal and rebellion will bring devouring by the sword. The LORD promises to avenge himself on adversaries, purge dross, and consume transgressors, sinners, and those who forsake him, who will burn like tinder and a spark with no one to quench them.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah / Chapter 1
s: The LORD commands the people to learn to do well, seek justice, relieve the oppressed, defend the fatherless, and plead for the widow. The city once full of justice, where righteousness lodged, now has murderers and princes who love bribes. The LORD promises to restore her judges and counselors so she will be called the city of righteousness, and to redeem Zion with justice and righteousness.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: Isaiah the son of Amoz records a vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem. In the latter days the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above all hills, nations will stream to it to learn the LORD's ways, and he will judge between them so that they beat swords into plowshares and stop learning war. The text then turns to the house of Jacob, which is accused of being filled with foreign divination, wealth, horses, chariots, and idols made by their own hands. A day of the LORD of Armies is announced against everything proud and lofty, including cedars, mountains, towers, walls, and ships of Tarshish, so that the LORD alone is exalted. Men will flee into rocks and caves in terror and cast away their silver and gold idols, and the chapter ends by urging people to stop trusting in man.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: Jerusalem is named with Judah as the subject of Isaiah's vision. It is the place from which the LORD's word will go out in the latter days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: The LORD will teach the peoples his ways and judge between the nations, bringing an end to war. He holds a coming day against all that is proud, and he alone will be exalted. When he arises to shake the earth mightily, men will hide from the terror of the LORD and the glory of his majesty.

l: house of prayer (the LORD's house), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: In the latter days it will be established on the top of the mountains and raised above the hills. All nations will flow to it, and people will say they will go up to it to be taught the God of Jacob's ways.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: The nations will flow to the LORD's mountain, and many peoples will go there to learn his ways and walk in his paths. The LORD will judge between them, and they will beat swords into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks, no longer lifting sword against each other or learning war.

l: house of Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: The house of Jacob is urged to walk in the light of the LORD. It is described as forsaken, filled with eastern practices and divination like the Philistines, and clasping hands with foreigners' children. Its land is full of silver, gold, horses, chariots, and idols.

l: idols, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: The land is full of idols that people worship, the work of their own hands and fingers. The text says idols shall utterly pass away, and in that day men will cast away their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats.

l: Day of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: It is a day of the LORD of Armies against all that is proud, arrogant, and lifted up, including cedars of Lebanon, oaks of Bashan, high mountains, towers, fortified walls, and ships of Tarshish. On it everything lofty is brought low and the LORD alone is exalted.

l: pride and arrogance of man, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: The lofty looks and arrogance of men will be bowed down and brought low, as the text states twice. Man is described as brought low and humbled, and the closing verse tells hearers to stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils.

l: men hiding from the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 2
s: Men are told to enter the rock and hide in the dust, and they are said to go into caves, holes of the earth, and clefts of ragged rocks. They flee from the terror of the LORD and the glory of his majesty when he arises to shake the earth mightily, casting away their idols as they go.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 describes the Lord, GOD of Armies, removing from Jerusalem and Judah all supply and support, including food, water, and capable leaders such as the mighty man, judge, prophet, and elder. Boys and children are given to rule, the people oppress one another, and the situation is so ruinous that no one will accept leadership. Jerusalem and Judah fall because their words and deeds defy the LORD and they flaunt their sin like Sodom, while the righteous are told it will go well for them and the wicked are told disaster awaits. The LORD stands to judge the elders and leaders for devouring the vineyard and plundering and crushing the poor. He then condemns the arrogant daughters of Zion, announcing sores and baldness, the loss of their finery, and a reversal into rottenness, rope, sackcloth, and branding, while their men fall by the sword and Jerusalem sits desolate on the ground.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The Lord, GOD of Armies, takes away supply and support, including bread, water, and leaders, from Jerusalem and Judah. He stands to contend and judge, accusing the elders and leaders of eating up the vineyard and crushing the poor. He also announces sores, baldness, and the removal of finery for the daughters of Zion.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem is said to be ruined because its tongue and doings are against the LORD. Its supplies and leaders are removed, and its gates will lament and mourn as she sits desolate on the ground.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: Judah is said to have fallen because their words and deeds provoke the eyes of the LORD's glory. Along with Jerusalem, it loses its supply, support, and leadership.

l: daughters of Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The daughters of Zion are called arrogant, walking with outstretched necks, flirting eyes, and jingling ornaments on their feet. The Lord will bring sores and baldness on them and strip away their jewelry and finery, replacing beauty with rottenness, rope, sackcloth, and branding.

l: people of Jerusalem and Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The people will be oppressed, each by another and by neighbor, and the child will act proudly against the old man. They display their sin like Sodom and bring disaster on themselves, though the righteous among them are told it will be well. Their men and mighty will fall by the sword in war.

l: leaders and elders (of Judah), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The mighty man, judge, prophet, elder, and other leaders are taken away. The LORD enters judgment with the elders and leaders, accusing them of eating up the vineyard, holding the plunder of the poor in their houses, and crushing and grinding the face of the poor. Those who lead the people are said to cause them to err and destroy the way of their paths.

l: boys and children (rulers of Judah), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The Lord gives boys as princes and children to rule over the people. Children are called the oppressors of the people, and a child behaves proudly against the old man.

l: adornments and finery (of the women of Zion), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: A long list of items is named, including anklets, headbands, crescent necklaces, earrings, bracelets, veils, rings, robes, mirrors, tiaras, and shawls. The Lord will take all of them away, and they will be replaced by rottenness, a rope, baldness, sackcloth, and branding.

l: Judgment and punishment of Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 3
s: The LORD stands to contend and judge, bringing disaster on the wicked so that the deeds of their hands are paid back to them. The punishment includes loss of food, water, and leaders, oppression, humiliation of the women of Zion, death by the sword, and desolation of Jerusalem. The righteous are told they will eat the fruit of their deeds and that it will be well with them.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 describes a future 'day' in which seven women take hold of one man, asking to be called by his name to remove their reproach while providing their own bread and clothing. The LORD's branch and the land's fruit will be beautiful and glorious for the survivors of Israel. Those left in Zion and Jerusalem, written among the living, will be called holy after the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and purges Jerusalem's blood by the spirit of justice and burning. The LORD will then create over Mount Zion and its assemblies a cloud and smoke by day and a flaming fire by night, forming a canopy of glory. This serves as a pavilion giving shade from heat and refuge from storm and rain.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD's branch is said to become beautiful and glorious in that day. He will create over all of Mount Zion and its assemblies a cloud and smoke by day and a shining flaming fire by night, as a canopy and pavilion of shade, refuge, and shelter.

l: seven women, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: Seven women take hold of one man in that day, saying they will eat their own bread and wear their own clothing. They ask only to be called by his name so that their reproach is taken away.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: Those who are left in Zion will be called holy, being written among the living. The Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will cover the whole habitation of Mount Zion with a protective canopy.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: Those who remain in Jerusalem will be called holy, as everyone written among the living there. Its blood will be purged from within it by the spirit of justice and the spirit of burning.

l: survivors of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: The fruit of the land will be the beauty and glory of the survivors of Israel in that day.

l: cloud and smoke (over Mount Zion), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: The LORD will create a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night, over the whole habitation of Mount Zion and her assemblies. It forms a canopy over all the glory, serving as a pavilion for shade from heat and as refuge and shelter from storm and rain.

l: purification of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 4
s: The Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion and purge the blood of Jerusalem from within it. This is done by the spirit of justice and the spirit of burning, after which the remnant will be called holy.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 opens with a song about a beloved's vineyard on a fruitful hill that was carefully cultivated yet yielded wild grapes, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah are asked to judge between him and it. He announces he will remove its hedge and wall, leave it a wasteland of briers and thorns, and withhold rain. The vineyard is identified as the house of Israel and the men of Judah, from whom the LORD of Armies looked for justice and righteousness but found oppression and a cry of distress. A series of woes follows against land-grabbers, drunken revelers, those who mock God's work, those who call evil good, the self-wise, and corrupt judges who take bribes. The chapter ends with the LORD's anger stretched out against his people and a distant nation summoned by a banner, swift and tireless, roaring like lions and leaving darkness and distress.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD of Armies is identified as the owner of the vineyard, which is the house of Israel, and he looked for justice and righteousness but found oppression and distress. He declares that he will remove the vineyard's protection, pronounces woes on the unjust, and is exalted in justice and sanctified in righteousness. His anger burns against his people, his hand remains stretched out, and he lifts a banner and whistles for a distant nation to come.

l: vineyard (the beloved's vineyard), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: The beloved's vineyard on a very fruitful hill was dug, cleared of stones, planted with the choicest vine, and given a tower and a wine press, yet it yielded wild grapes. The beloved announces he will take away its hedge and wall so it is eaten up and trampled, make it a wasteland of briers and thorns, and command the clouds not to rain on it. It is then explained to be the house of Israel and the men of Judah.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: The house of Israel is identified as the vineyard of the LORD of Armies. He looked for justice from it but found oppression, and for righteousness but found a cry of distress.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: The men of Judah, with the inhabitants of Jerusalem, are asked to judge between the beloved and his vineyard. They are named as his pleasant plant, from which he looked for justice and found oppression.

l: those who join house to house (land-grabbers), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: Those who join house to house and lay field to field until there is no room are met with a woe, and are told they will dwell alone in the middle of the land. The LORD says many great and beautiful houses will be desolate and unoccupied, and that ten acres of vineyard will yield only one bath.

l: drunken revelers, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: Those who rise early to follow strong drink and stay late until wine inflames them are met with a woe. They have harp, lyre, tambourine, flute, and wine at their feasts but do not respect or consider the work of the LORD. Those mighty at drinking wine and mixing strong drink are also condemned, and Sheol opens its mouth wide to take their glory and multitude.

l: those who call evil good (the corrupt and arrogant), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: Woes are pronounced on those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, mock the Holy One's work, call evil good and good evil, and are wise in their own eyes. Also condemned are those who acquit the guilty for a bribe and deny justice to the innocent. Because they rejected the law of the LORD of Armies and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel, their root will rot and their blossom go up as dust.

l: distant nations (invaders), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: The LORD lifts a banner and whistles for a nation from far away, and they come speedily and swiftly. They are tireless, with sharp arrows, bent bows, horses with hoofs like flint, and wheels like a whirlwind. They roar like lions, seize their prey with no one to deliver it, and bring darkness and distress to the land.

l: judgment and desolation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 5
s: Judgment comes as a stripped and wasted vineyard, desolate houses, meager harvests, famine and thirst, captivity, and Sheol swallowing the proud. The people are consumed like stubble in fire, the mountains tremble, dead bodies lie as refuse in the streets, and the LORD's anger is not turned away. The chapter closes with invasion and a land of darkness and distress.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: In the year King Uzziah died, the narrator sees the Lord enthroned in the temple, attended by six-winged seraphim who proclaim the holiness of the LORD of Armies. The narrator is overwhelmed by his own uncleanness and that of his people, until one of the seraphim touches his mouth with a live coal from the altar and declares his iniquity taken away. When the Lord asks whom he should send, the narrator volunteers, and is told to go to this people with a message that they will hear and see without understanding, their hearts made fat, ears heavy and eyes shut so they do not turn and be healed. Asked how long, he is told until cities, houses and land are utterly waste and the people removed far away, with even a surviving tenth to be consumed, leaving the holy seed as a stump like that of a terebinth or oak.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: The LORD of Armies is the King whom the narrator sees enthroned, with his train filling the temple. The seraphim declare him holy, holy, holy and say the whole earth is full of his glory. He asks whom to send and commissions the narrator with a message of hardening, and he describes the coming desolation of the land.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: The narrator sees the Lord on a throne and cries out that he is undone, a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips. After a seraph touches his mouth with a live coal and declares his sin forgiven, he answers the Lord's call with 'Here I am. Send me!' He is told to give this people a message they will not understand and asks 'Lord, how long?'

l: seraphim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: The seraphim stand above the Lord, each with six wings: two cover the face, two cover the feet, and two are for flying. They call to one another that the LORD of Armies is holy and that the earth is full of his glory. One of them flies to the narrator with a live coal from the altar, taken with tongs, touches his mouth, and pronounces his iniquity taken away.

l: this people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: This people is described by the narrator as having unclean lips. They are the audience of the message to hear but not understand and to see but not perceive, with hearts made fat, ears heavy and eyes shut so that they do not turn and be healed. The Lord says they will be removed far away, and even a remaining tenth will be consumed.

l: Isaiah's commission to a hardening message, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: After the Lord asks whom to send, the narrator volunteers and is told to go and tell this people that they hear but do not understand and see but do not perceive. The message is to make their hearts fat, their ears heavy and their eyes shut, lest they understand and turn and be healed. When he asks how long, he is told it lasts until the land is utterly waste.

l: Isaiah's vision of the Lord, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: In the year King Uzziah died, the narrator sees the Lord sitting on a high and lifted-up throne, his train filling the temple. Seraphim above him cry out his holiness, the thresholds' foundations shake at the voice, and the house fills with smoke. The sight makes the narrator declare himself undone because his eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies.

l: cleansing of Isaiah's lips, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: A seraph flies to the narrator with a live coal taken with tongs from the altar. He touches the narrator's mouth with it and says that it has touched his lips, his iniquity is taken away, and his sin forgiven. This answers the narrator's cry that he is a man of unclean lips.

l: coming desolation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 6
s: In answer to 'how long?', the Lord says it will last until cities are waste without inhabitant, houses without man, and the land utterly waste. The LORD will have removed men far away and the forsaken places will be many within the land. Even a surviving tenth will be consumed, like a terebinth or oak whose stump remains, and the holy seed is that stump.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: In the days of King Ahaz of Judah, Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah of Israel went up against Jerusalem but could not prevail, and Ahaz and his people trembled when told Syria was allied with Ephraim. The LORD sent Isaiah and his son Shearjashub to meet Ahaz and tell him not to fear, because the plot to tear Judah apart and set up the son of Tabeel as king would not stand, and Ephraim would be broken within sixty-five years. The LORD then told Ahaz to ask for a sign, but Ahaz refused, saying he would not tempt the LORD. The LORD himself therefore gave a sign: the virgin will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, and before the child knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land of the two kings will be forsaken. The chapter ends by foretelling that the LORD will bring the king of Assyria, along with flies and bees, on Judah, leaving the land desolate and overgrown with briers and thorns.

l: Ahaz, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Ahaz, king of Judah and descendant of David, trembled with his people when told Syria was allied with Ephraim. The LORD told him through Isaiah not to fear and offered him a sign, but Ahaz refused, saying he would not tempt the LORD. The LORD then declared that days of trouble, including the king of Assyria, would come on him, his people, and his father's house.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Isaiah was commanded by the LORD to meet Ahaz with his son Shearjashub at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field. He was to tell Ahaz to keep calm and not fear Rezin and the son of Remaliah, since their plot would not stand.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD sent Isaiah to reassure Ahaz that the plot of Syria and Ephraim would not stand, and offered Ahaz a sign in the depth or the height. When Ahaz refused, the LORD himself gave the sign of Immanuel. He also announced he would whistle for the fly of Egypt and the bee of Assyria and bring the king of Assyria on Judah.

l: Rezin, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Rezin, king of Syria, went up with Pekah to Jerusalem to war against it but could not prevail. The LORD said his fierce anger is like the smoking tails of torches, and that he is the head of Damascus, which is the head of Syria.

l: Pekah the son of Remaliah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Pekah, called the son of Remaliah and king of Israel, joined Rezin in going up against Jerusalem without prevailing. He is described as the head of Samaria and as a co-plotter who planned to tear Judah apart and set up the son of Tabeel as king.

l: Syria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Syria, with its head in Damascus under Rezin, allied with Ephraim and plotted evil against Judah. The LORD declared that the plot would not stand or happen.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Ephraim was reported to be allied with Syria and joined the plot to divide Judah. The LORD said that within sixty-five years Ephraim would be broken in pieces so that it would no longer be a people, and that its head is Samaria, whose head is Remaliah's son.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Judah was attacked by Syria and Ephraim, who plotted to tear it apart, divide it, and set up the son of Tabeel as king, but they could not prevail. Later its land is foretold to be overrun by Assyria and to become briers and thorns, with vineyards lost and hills used only for oxen and sheep.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: The king of Assyria is foretold as the one the LORD will bring on Ahaz, his people, and his father's house, in days unlike any since Ephraim departed from Judah. The LORD will whistle for the bee in Assyria's land, and the king of Assyria is likened to a hired razor that shaves the head, the hair of the feet, and the beard.

l: Immanuel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: Immanuel is the name to be given to the son the virgin will conceive and bear. Before he knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land whose two kings Ahaz abhors will be forsaken, and he will eat butter and honey.

l: virgin (the sign), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: The virgin is said to be the one who will conceive, bear a son, and call his name Immanuel. She is the central figure of the sign the LORD himself gives to the house of David.

l: sign, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 7
s: The LORD told Ahaz to ask a sign in the depth or the height, but Ahaz declined. The LORD then gave the sign himself: the virgin will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, whose early growth is tied to the forsaking of the land of the two kings.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The LORD instructs the speaker to write 'For Maher Shalal Hash Baz' on a large tablet before witnesses Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberechiah, and a son is born to the speaker and the prophetess and given that name as a sign that Damascus and Samaria will be plundered by the king of Assyria. Because this people refused the waters of Shiloah and rejoiced in Rezin and Remaliah's son, the LORD will bring the king of Assyria like a mighty flood of the River that sweeps into Judah, reaching to the neck, though the peoples who plot against it are told they will be shattered because God is with us. The LORD warns the speaker not to walk in the way of this people or fear what they fear, but to hold the LORD of Armies as holy, who will be a sanctuary to some and a stumbling stone, trap and snare to both houses of Israel and the people of Jerusalem. The speaker is told to bind up the covenant and seal the law among his disciples, and he resolves to wait for the LORD who hides his face from the house of Jacob. He and his children are signs in Israel, and the people are urged to turn to the law and covenant rather than consult mediums and wizards, or they will have no morning and will be driven into thick darkness, hungry and cursing their king and their God.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The LORD instructs the speaker to write on a tablet, names the child Maher Shalal Hash Baz, and announces that he will bring the king of Assyria as a flood upon this people. He commands the speaker not to follow this people's ways or fears but to regard the LORD of Armies as holy, who will be a sanctuary and also a stumbling stone, trap and snare. He is described as hiding his face from the house of Jacob and dwelling in Mount Zion.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The speaker, addressed by the LORD, takes a tablet, has witnesses, goes to the prophetess, and fathers a son who is named Maher Shalal Hash Baz. He is warned with a strong hand not to walk in the way of this people, is told to wrap up the covenant and seal the law among his disciples, and resolves to wait for and look for the LORD. He declares that he and the children the LORD gave him are signs and wonders in Israel.

l: Maher Shalal Hash Baz, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: This is the name written on the large tablet and given to the son born to the speaker and the prophetess. The LORD says that before the child can say 'My father' and 'My mother,' the riches of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried away by the king of Assyria.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The king of Assyria is foretold to carry away the riches of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria before the child can speak. He is identified with the mighty flood waters of the River, coming with all his glory as the LORD's instrument against this people.

l: the River, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The invasion is pictured as the mighty flood waters of the River, rising over all its channels and banks. It sweeps into Judah, overflows and passes through, reaches to the neck, and its outstretched wings fill the width of the land of Immanuel.

l: this people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: This people is charged with refusing the waters of Shiloah that go softly and rejoicing in Rezin and Remaliah's son, and so will be overwhelmed by the flood. The speaker is told not to walk in their way, call a conspiracy what they call a conspiracy, or fear their threats. They are tempted to consult mediums and wizards, and if they do not follow the law they face hunger, distress, cursing their king and God, and thick darkness.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: Judah is the land the Assyrian flood will sweep into, overflow and pass through, reaching to the neck. Its land is addressed as belonging to Immanuel, and the stretching wings of the flood will fill its width.

l: covenant and law, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: The speaker is told to wrap up the covenant and seal the law among his disciples. The people are urged to turn to the law and the covenant, and those who do not speak according to this word are said to have no morning.

l: mediums and wizards, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 8
s: Those with familiar spirits and wizards, who chirp and mutter, are the ones people urge others to consult. The text rebukes this, asking whether a people should not consult their God instead and whether they should consult the dead on behalf of the living.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 9
s: Chapter 9 opens with a promise that gloom will end for Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee of the nations, where people who walked in darkness see a great light. The nation is given increased joy, and the yoke, staff, and rod of the oppressor are broken as in the day of Midian. A child is born and a son given, bearing the names Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace, whose government on David's throne will have no end, upheld by the zeal of the LORD of Armies. The chapter then turns to judgment: the Lord sends a word against Jacob and Israel, and Ephraim and Samaria's proud boasts of rebuilding are answered by adversaries such as the Syrians and Philistines devouring Israel. Because the people do not turn to the LORD of Armies, he cuts off head and tail, wickedness burns like fire, people turn on one another, and Manasseh and Ephraim devour each other and together oppose Judah, while his anger is not turned away.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 9
s: The LORD of Armies is said to perform the establishment of the child's everlasting government through his zeal. He also acts in judgment: he is sought by no one among the people, his wrath burns up the land, and his anger is not turned away, with his hand stretched out still.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 9
s: Israel receives a word sent by the Lord and is devoured by the Syrians in front and the Philistines behind. The LORD cuts off its head and tail in one day, and its people, led astray by their leaders, become fuel for the fire of his wrath, with no one sparing his brother.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 9
s: Ephraim, along with the inhabitants of Samaria, speaks in pride, vowing to rebuild with cut stone and cedars after the bricks and sycamore fig trees fall. It is later described as eating Manasseh while Manasseh eats Ephraim, and together they are against Judah.

l: Immanuel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 9
s: A child is born and a son is given to us, and the government will be on his shoulders. He is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace, and his government on David's throne will increase without end, upheld with justice and righteousness forever.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 opens with woe pronounced on those who write unrighteous decrees that rob the needy, widows, and fatherless of justice, and asks what they will do in the day of visitation. The Lord then calls Assyria the rod of his anger, sent against a profane nation to plunder it, though Assyria does not intend to serve God and boasts of its own strength, wisdom, and conquests, comparing Jerusalem to the cities and idols it has already taken. God declares that after finishing his work on Mount Zion and Jerusalem he will punish the king of Assyria's arrogance, and compares Assyria's boasting to an ax or saw exalting itself over the one who wields it. The light of Israel will burn Assyria's forest like fire, leaving so few trees that a child could count them, while a remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God and lean on the LORD in truth. The Lord tells his people in Zion not to fear Assyria, promises that its yoke will be broken, traces Assyria's advance town by town to Nob near Jerusalem, and ends with the Lord cutting down the lofty like the forest, with Lebanon falling by the Mighty One.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: The Lord pronounces woe on unjust decree writers and calls Assyria the rod of his anger, sending it against a profane nation. He declares he will finish his work on Zion and Jerusalem, then punish the king of Assyria's pride, kindling a fire among Assyria's fat ones and cutting down its forest. He saves a remnant of Jacob, tells Zion not to fear Assyria, promises to stir up a scourge against it, and will lop the lofty with terror.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: Assyria is called the rod of the Lord's anger and is sent to take plunder and trample a profane nation, though it does not intend to serve God's purpose and aims only to destroy many nations. It boasts of conquests and moves through Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, and other towns to halt at Nob and shake its hand at Jerusalem. The Lord promises to punish its king, burn its forest down to a countable remnant, direct anger at its destruction, and break its burden and yoke from Zion's people.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: Israel is described as numerous as the sand of the sea, yet only a remnant will return after a destruction determined and overflowing with righteousness. The remnant of Israel and the escaped of the house of Jacob will no longer lean on the one who struck them but on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. The Lord's people in Zion are told not to fear Assyria, since its yoke will be destroyed and its burden removed.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: Jerusalem is compared by Assyria's boast to Samaria and the idol-worshiping cities it has conquered, and the Lord asks whether he will do to Jerusalem and her idols what he did to Samaria. He says he will perform his whole work on Mount Zion and Jerusalem before punishing Assyria's king. Assyria's advance ends at Nob, where it shakes its hand at the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.

l: unjust rulers and decree writers, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: They are met with woe for decreeing unrighteous decrees and writing oppressive ones that deprive the needy of justice and rob the poor of their rights. Through them widows become plunder and the fatherless become prey. They are asked what they will do in the day of visitation, to whom they will flee, and where they will leave their wealth; they will bow down under prisoners and fall among the slain.

l: profane nation (Israel), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: The profane nation is the people who anger the Lord, against whom he sends Assyria with a command to take plunder and prey and tread them down like the mire of the streets. The text compares its idols to those of the kingdoms Assyria has already found, and the Lord says he will do to Jerusalem and her idols as he did to Samaria. His anger is not turned away and his hand is stretched out still.

l: Assyria's pride and boasting, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: Assyria's king claims that all his princes are kings, that he acted by the strength of his hand and his wisdom, removed boundaries, robbed treasures, and gathered the earth like abandoned eggs with no one to chirp. The Lord says he will punish the fruit of his willful proud heart and the insolence of his arrogant looks after finishing his work on Zion and Jerusalem. The boast is answered with a fire that consumes Assyria's glory, fat ones, and forest.

l: ax, saw, rod and staff (tool analogy), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 10
s: The Lord asks whether an ax should brag against the one who chops with it, or a saw exalt itself above the one who saws with it. He adds that a rod lifting those who lift it, or a staff lifting someone who is not wood, would be equally absurd. The analogy shows that Assyria, the rod of his anger, is merely an instrument in his hand and has no ground for boasting.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 describes a shoot that will come from the stock of Jesse, on whom the LORD's Spirit rests with wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. He will judge the poor and humble with righteousness and equity, strike the wicked, and wear righteousness and faithfulness as his belt. Peace will extend to the animal world, where predators and prey, including the wolf, lamb, leopard, lion and cobra, live together with a little child leading them, since the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD. In that day the nations will seek the root of Jesse, and the Lord will a second time recover the remnant of his people from Assyria, Egypt and other lands, ending the rivalry of Ephraim and Judah. The LORD will dry up obstacles such as the Egyptian sea and the River, making a highway for the remnant from Assyria as there was for Israel out of Egypt.

l: Jesse, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Jesse is named as the source of a shoot that will come out of his stock and a branch from his roots that will bear fruit. His root will stand as a banner of the peoples, which the nations will seek, and his resting place will be glorious.

l: shoot (from the stock of Jesse), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: The shoot will have the LORD's Spirit resting on him: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. He will delight in the fear of the LORD, judge not by sight or hearing but with righteousness and equity for the poor and humble, strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and kill the wicked with the breath of his lips. Righteousness and faithfulness will be his belt.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: The LORD's Spirit rests on the shoot from Jesse, and his holy mountain will be free of hurt and destruction. In that day the Lord will set his hand a second time to recover the remnant of his people and set up a banner for the nations. He will utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea, wave his hand with a scorching wind over the River and split it into seven streams so men can cross in sandals.

l: animals (wolf, lamb, leopard, lion, etc.), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat, with the calf, young lion and fattened calf together, led by a little child. The cow and bear will graze, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. Nursing and weaned children will play safely near the cobra's hole and viper's den.

l: remnant of the LORD's people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: The remnant that is left of the LORD's people will be recovered a second time from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath and the islands of the sea. A highway will be made for them from Assyria, like the one Israel had when it came up out of the land of Egypt.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Assyria is named as one of the places from which the Lord will recover the remnant of his people. A highway will be provided for the remnant that is left from Assyria.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Egypt is named as a place from which the Lord will recover his people's remnant. The LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and the earlier day when Israel came up out of the land of Egypt serves as the comparison for the new highway.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Judah's dispersed will be gathered from the four corners of the earth. Those who persecute Judah will be cut off, and Judah will not persecute Ephraim. Judah, together with Ephraim, will fly down on the shoulders of the Philistines, plunder the children of the east, and extend power over Edom and Moab, while the children of Ammon obey them.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: Ephraim's envy will depart, and Ephraim will not envy Judah. The text presents the two as reconciled and acting together against the Philistines, the children of the east, Edom, Moab and Ammon.

l: righteous reign of the shoot, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: The shoot's rule is marked by judgment based on righteousness and equity rather than appearances, favoring the poor and humble and striking down the wicked. It is accompanied by peace among animals and people, with no hurt or destruction on the LORD's holy mountain, because the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

l: gathering of the remnant, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 11
s: In that day the Lord will set his hand a second time to recover his people's remnant and will raise a banner for the nations to assemble Israel's outcasts and Judah's dispersed from the four corners of the earth. The LORD will remove barriers by splitting the River into seven streams and will make a highway for the remnant to return.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 presents a short song of thanksgiving that the people will sing "in that day." In the first part, the speaker thanks the LORD because his anger has turned away and he now comforts them, and declares trust in God as salvation, strength, and song. The people will joyfully draw water from the wells of salvation. In the second part, they are called to give thanks to the LORD, call on his name, declare his deeds among the peoples, and sing of the excellent things he has done so it is known in all the earth. The chapter closes by urging the inhabitant of Zion to cry aloud and shout because the Holy One of Israel is great among them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 12
s: The LORD is thanked because his anger has turned away and he comforts the people. He is described as their strength and song, and as having become their salvation. He is to be praised, called on, and proclaimed as exalted among the peoples and in all the earth for his excellent deeds.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 12
s: Zion is the place whose inhabitant is told to cry aloud and shout. It is where the Holy One of Israel is great, being present among its people.

l: inhabitant of Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 12
s: The inhabitant of Zion is addressed in the final verse and commanded to cry aloud and shout. The reason given is that the Holy One of Israel is great among them.

l: salvation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 12
s: Salvation is identified with God, who is said to be the speaker's salvation and to have become it. It is also pictured as wells from which people will joyfully draw water.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 is a prophecy about Babylon, seen by Isaiah the son of Amoz. The LORD of Armies musters an army from far countries to carry out his anger, and the coming day of the LORD is described as cruel, with cosmic darkening and the shaking of heaven and earth. The people face terror, slaughter, and plunder, and the LORD says he will stir up the Medes against them. Babylon, called the glory of kingdoms, is to be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah and left permanently uninhabited, home only to desert animals. Its time is said to be near.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: Babylon is the subject of the burden Isaiah saw, called the glory of kingdoms and the beauty of the Chaldeans' pride. It will be overthrown as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and will never be inhabited again, with only jackals, ostriches, hyenas, and wild goats living there. Its time is near and its days will not be prolonged.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: The LORD of Armies musters the army for battle and commands his consecrated ones and mighty men for his anger. He says he will punish the world for its evil, end the arrogance of the proud, make people rarer than gold, shake heaven and earth, and stir up the Medes against Babylon.

l: Medes, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: The Medes are the people the LORD says he will stir up against Babylon's people. They will not value silver or delight in gold, and their bows will dash young men in pieces. They will show no pity on children or the fruit of the womb.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: The day of the LORD is described as at hand and coming as destruction from the Almighty, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger. It will make the land a desolation and destroy its sinners. The stars, sun, and moon will lose their light, and the heavens and earth will tremble and shake in his fierce anger.

l: army of the nations (mustered by the LORD), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: A noise like a great people and an uproar of gathered kingdoms of nations is heard in the mountains as the LORD of Armies musters the army for battle. They come from a far country, from the uttermost part of heaven, as the weapons of his indignation to destroy the whole land.

l: inhabitants of Babylon's land, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 13
s: The inhabitants are told to wail, and their hands will be feeble and their hearts will melt. They will be in pain like a woman in labor, with faces of flame, and will flee like hunted gazelles to their own people and lands. Those found or captured will be killed by the sword, their infants dashed in pieces, their houses ransacked, and their wives raped.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 promises that the LORD will have compassion on Jacob, choose Israel again, and set them in their own land, where foreigners will join them and their former oppressors will serve them. Israel is told to take up a parable against the king of Babylon, who is mocked as a fallen oppressor: Sheol stirs the dead rulers to greet him, and the shining one who vowed to ascend to heaven and make himself like the Most High is brought down to the pit. He is denied honorable burial, his offspring are marked for slaughter, and the LORD of Armies vows to cut off Babylon's name and remnant and make it a possession for the porcupine and pools of water. The LORD also swears to break the Assyrian in his land and declares his plan for all nations, which no one can stop. In a burden dated to the year King Ahaz died, Philistia is warned not to rejoice over a broken rod, since worse will come out of the north, while Zion is affirmed as founded by the LORD as a refuge for the afflicted.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD is said to have compassion on Jacob, to choose Israel again, and to break the staff of the wicked. As the LORD of Armies he vows to cut off Babylon's name and remnant, to break the Assyrian in his land, and to kill Philistia's root with famine. He swears that his purpose will stand and that no one can stop or turn back his outstretched hand, and he has founded Zion.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Jacob is the object of the LORD's compassion, and the house of Jacob will be united with foreigners who join themselves to it. This is part of the promise of restoration to their own land.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Israel will be chosen again by the LORD and set in its own land. The house of Israel will possess peoples as servants and handmaids, take captive those who held it captive, and rule over its oppressors. It is told to take up a parable against the king of Babylon.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: The king of Babylon is mocked in a parable as an oppressor who struck the peoples in wrath and who has now ceased. He is addressed as the shining one, son of the dawn, who said in his heart he would ascend to heaven and make himself like the Most High, but is brought down to Sheol and the pit. He is denied burial with other kings and cast out like an abominable branch because he destroyed his land and killed his people, and his offspring are to be slaughtered.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD of Armies declares he will rise against Babylon and cut off its name, remnant, son and son's son. He will make it a possession for the porcupine and pools of water and sweep it with the broom of destruction.

l: Sheol, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Sheol is portrayed as stirring from beneath to meet the king of Babylon at his coming, raising the departed spirits and the former rulers from their thrones. The dead ask whether he has become as weak as they are, and his pomp and the sound of his stringed instruments are brought down there, with maggots and worms covering him.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD swears to break the Assyrian in his land and tread him underfoot on his mountains. Then the Assyrian's yoke and burden will leave the shoulders of the people.

l: Philistia, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Philistia is told not to rejoice that the rod that struck it is broken, because an adder and a fiery flying serpent will come from the serpent's root. The LORD will kill its root with famine and its remnant will be killed. It is told to howl as it melts away because smoke comes out of the north.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 14
s: Zion is said to have been founded by the LORD. The afflicted of his people will take refuge in her, and this is the answer to give the messengers of the nation.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 15
s: Chapter 15 delivers a burden, or oracle, against Moab. Its cities Ar and Kir are laid waste in a single night. The people go to high places such as Bayith and Dibon to weep, shave their heads and beards, and wear sackcloth, while cries ring from Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, and across Moab's borders. Nobles flee toward Zoar and Horonaim, the waters of Nimrim dry up, and survivors carry off their stored goods over the brook of the willows. The speaker laments for Moab, yet declares the waters of Dimon full of blood and promises still more on Dimon, a lion against those of Moab who escape and the remnant of the land.

l: Moab, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 15
s: Moab is the subject of the burden. Its cities Ar and Kir are laid waste in a night, its people wail over Nebo and Medeba, and its armed men cry aloud with trembling souls. Its nobles flee, its land withers, and a lion is promised against those who escape and the remnant of the land.

l: destruction of Moab, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 15
s: Ar of Moab and Kir of Moab are laid waste and brought to nothing in a single night. The waters of Nimrim become desolate and the grass withers, and survivors carry off their stored goods over the brook of the willows. The waters of Dimon are full of blood, with yet more promised on Dimon and a lion on those who escape and on the remnant of the land.

l: mourning of Moab, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 15
s: Moab goes up to Bayith, Dibon, and the high places to weep and wails over Nebo and Medeba, with every head bald and every beard cut off. In the streets and on the housetops people wear sackcloth and weep abundantly. Heshbon, Elealeh, and Jahaz echo with the cry, which goes around Moab's borders to Eglaim and Beer Elim, and the speaker's own heart cries out for Moab.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: Chapter 16 continues the oracle concerning Moab. Moabite daughters are pictured as scattered birds at the fords of the Arnon, and an appeal is made for Zion to hide the outcasts and fugitive from the destroyer, with the promise that oppression will end and a throne will be established in loving kindness in the tent of David. The speaker then reports Moab's pride, arrogance and wrath, which come to nothing, and describes Moab wailing over the ruined vineyards and fields of Heshbon, Sibmah, Jazer, Elealeh and Kir Hareseth. The speaker weeps and mourns for Moab, and Moab's prayers at the high place and sanctuary will not prevail. The LORD concludes that within three years the glory of Moab and its great multitude will be held in contempt, leaving a very small and feeble remnant.

l: Moab, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: Moab is pictured as wandering birds and a scattered nest, with its daughters at the fords of the Arnon. It wails over its ruined vineyards and fields, and when it goes to its high place and sanctuary to pray, it will not prevail.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD is identified as the one who spoke the word against Moab in time past. He now declares that within three years Moab's glory will be brought into contempt, leaving only a small and feeble remnant.

l: outcasts and fugitive (Moabite refugees), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: The outcasts and fugitive are those for whom shelter is requested: they are to be hidden, not betrayed, and allowed to dwell with Zion. Moab is to find a hiding place from the face of the destroyer.

l: righteous king (throne in the tent of David), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: A throne will be established in loving kindness, and one will sit on it in truth in the tent of David. He will judge, seek justice, and be swift to do righteousness, in a time when the extortionist, destruction and the oppressors are gone.

l: Moab's pride, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: It is reported that Moab is very proud, marked by arrogance, pride and wrath. His boastings are declared to be nothing.

l: Moab's coming downfall within three years, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 16
s: The LORD fixes the timing: within three years, counted as a contract worker would count them, Moab's glory and great multitude will be brought into contempt. The remnant will be very small and feeble.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: Chapter 17 delivers the LORD of Armies' burden against Damascus, which is to become a ruinous heap while its cities are abandoned to flocks. The fortress of Ephraim and the kingdom of Damascus, along with the remnant of Syria, will cease. The glory of Jacob will grow thin like a field stripped by the harvester, leaving only a few gleanings like olives left on a shaken tree. In that day people will look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel, and not to altars, Asherah poles or incense altars, because they forgot the God of their salvation and planted foreign seedlings whose harvest flees in grief. The chapter ends with the roar of many peoples and nations, whom God rebukes so that they flee like chaff and dust, and with the plunderers of the speaker's people vanishing before morning.

l: Damascus, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: Damascus is declared to be taken away from being a city and to become a ruinous heap. Its kingdom is to cease, and its cities are to be forsaken and left for flocks to lie down in without fear.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: Ephraim's fortress is said to cease, along with the kingdom of Damascus and the remnant of Syria. This places Ephraim in the same coming judgment as Damascus.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: The LORD of Armies, also called the LORD, the God of Israel, speaks the burden against Damascus and announces the fading of Jacob's glory. He is the Maker and Holy One to whom people will look in that day. He rebukes the roaring nations so that they flee like chaff before the wind.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: The glory of Jacob will be made thin and the fatness of his flesh will become lean. He is compared to a field after harvest, with only a few gleanings remaining, like two or three olives left on the top bough of a shaken tree.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: The glory of the children of Israel is the standard to which Damascus's remnant is compared in verse 3. Their forsaken places in the woods and on the mountain top are also the comparison for the strong cities that will become a desolation.

l: many peoples and nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: Many peoples and nations roar and rush like the seas and mighty waters. The LORD rebukes them, and they flee far off, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and like whirling dust before the storm.

l: plunderers (those who plunder us), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: Those who plunder and rob the speaker's people bring terror at evening but are gone before morning. This is called their portion and their lot.

l: people of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: In that day people will look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel, and no longer to altars, Asherah poles or incense altars made by their own hands. They are accused of forgetting the God of their salvation and the rock of their strength, planting pleasant plants and foreign seedlings whose harvest flees in the day of grief and desperate sorrow. Their strong cities will become desolate like forsaken places.

l: judgment on Damascus, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 17
s: The judgment is announced as a burden in which Damascus becomes a ruinous heap and its cities are abandoned to flocks. It also ends the fortress of Ephraim and the kingdom of Damascus and the remnant of Syria, and it is tied to a wider reckoning that thins Jacob's glory and turns people from idols.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: Chapter 18 opens with an address to a land of the rustling of wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by sea in papyrus vessels to a nation tall and smooth. All the world's inhabitants are called to look and listen when a banner is raised on the mountains and a trumpet is blown. The LORD tells the speaker that he will remain still and watch from his dwelling place, like clear heat in sunshine or a cloud of dew in harvest heat. Before the harvest, he will cut off the sprigs and spreading branches of the vine with pruning hooks, leaving them for ravenous birds and animals to eat through summer and winter. At that time a present will be brought to the LORD of Armies from the tall and smooth people to Mount Zion.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: The LORD tells the speaker that he will be still and watch from his dwelling place, like clear heat in sunshine or a cloud of dew in harvest heat. He will cut off the sprigs and spreading branches with pruning hooks before the harvest. He is also called the LORD of Armies, and receives a present at Mount Zion.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: Mount Zion is identified as the place of the name of the LORD of Armies. It is the destination to which the present from the tall and smooth people will be brought.

l: nation tall and smooth, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: This nation is described as awesome from its beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide. It receives ambassadors sent by swift messengers in papyrus vessels, and at that time it will bring a present to the LORD of Armies at Mount Zion.

l: land of the rustling of wings, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: This land is addressed with 'Ah' and is located beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. It sends ambassadors by sea in vessels of papyrus on the waters, saying 'Go, you swift messengers' to a nation tall and smooth.

l: harvest, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: The harvest is the setting for the LORD's stillness, likened to a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. Before it, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, the LORD will cut off the sprigs and branches.

l: sprigs and spreading branches (of the vine), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: The LORD will cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks and cut down and take away the spreading branches, before the harvest and once the flower has become a ripening grape. They will be left together for the ravenous birds of the mountains and the animals of the earth, which will eat them in summer and winter respectively.

l: present (brought to the LORD of Armies), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 18
s: A present will be brought to the LORD of Armies in that time. It comes from the tall and smooth people, the nation that measures out and treads down, and is brought to Mount Zion, the place of the LORD's name.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: Chapter 19 delivers the burden of Egypt. The LORD comes on a swift cloud, shaking Egypt's idols, stirring Egyptians to civil strife, and giving them over to a cruel lord and fierce king. The Nile and its streams dry up, ruining fishermen, flax workers, and weavers, while the princes of Zoan and Memphis, and Pharaoh's counselors, are shown to be foolish and misled by a perverse spirit. In that day Egypt will tremble, five Egyptian cities will speak the language of Canaan and swear to the LORD, and an altar and pillar will mark his presence. The LORD will strike and heal Egypt, a highway will link Egypt and Assyria so they worship together, and Israel will be a third with them as a blessing, each named as the LORD's own.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: The LORD of Armies comes to Egypt on a swift cloud, stirs up its people against one another, destroys their counsel, and mixes a spirit of perverseness among them. He gives Egypt to a cruel lord, strikes and heals it, and becomes known to the Egyptians, who vow and sacrifice to him. He finally blesses Egypt as his people, Assyria as the work of his hands, and Israel as his inheritance.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: Egypt faces the LORD's judgment: its idols tremble, its heart melts, its waters and Nile fields dry up, and its work and counsel fail. Afterward it receives an altar and a pillar to the LORD, five cities that speak the language of Canaan, a savior and defender, and healing. It is called 'my people' and joined with Assyria and Israel.

l: Egyptians, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: The Egyptians are stirred to fight brother against brother and city against city, lose their spirit, and turn to idols, charmers, and wizards. They are given to a fierce king, become like women trembling at the LORD's shaking hand, and fear Judah. In that day they cry to the LORD, know him, worship with sacrifice and offering, keep their vows, return to him, are healed, and worship with the Assyrians.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: Assyria appears in the promise that a highway will run from Egypt to Assyria, with the Assyrian entering Egypt and the Egyptian entering Assyria. The Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. The LORD calls Assyria 'the work of my hands.'

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: Israel is promised that in that day it will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing within the earth. The LORD names Israel 'my inheritance.' The land of Judah is also said to become a terror to Egypt.

l: burden of Egypt (judgment and restoration), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 19
s: The burden of Egypt opens with judgment: civil strife, a cruel ruler, a failing Nile, and foolish counselors in Zoan and Memphis misled by a perverse spirit. It turns in 'that day' to restoration, with Egyptian worship of the LORD, deliverance from oppressors, striking and healing, and a shared blessing with Assyria and Israel.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: In the year Tartan, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and captured it, the LORD told Isaiah son of Amoz to loosen the sackcloth from his waist and remove his sandals, and Isaiah walked naked and barefoot. The LORD explained that Isaiah's three years of walking this way were a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and Ethiopia. The king of Assyria would lead away the captives of Egypt and exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot with buttocks uncovered, to Egypt's shame. Egypt and Ethiopia would be dismayed and confounded, since Ethiopia was their expectation and Egypt their glory. The inhabitants of the coast land would then say that those they had fled to for help against the king of Assyria were captured, and ask how they themselves would escape.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: Assyria's king Sargon sent Tartan, who fought against Ashdod and took it. The LORD says the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, to Egypt's shame.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: The LORD spoke by Isaiah, commanding him to loosen his sackcloth and remove his sandals. He declared Isaiah's three years of walking naked and barefoot a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and Ethiopia, and announced that Assyria would lead them away captive.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: Isaiah, son of Amoz, is told by the LORD to loosen the sackcloth from his waist and take off his sandals, and he does so, walking naked and barefoot. The LORD calls him his servant and says he has walked this way three years as a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and Ethiopia.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: Egypt is the subject of the sign: its captives will be led away by the king of Assyria naked and barefoot, to Egypt's shame. Egypt is called a glory in which people had hope, and its people will be dismayed and confounded.

l: Ethiopia, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: Ethiopia is a subject of the sign, and its exiles will be led away by the king of Assyria, young and old, naked and barefoot. It is described as an expectation that will leave people dismayed and confounded.

l: captives and exiles of Egypt and Ethiopia, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: The captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, will be led away by the king of Assyria. They will be naked and barefoot with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.

l: inhabitants (of this coast land), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: The inhabitants of this coast land will say in that day that Egypt and Ethiopia were their expectation, where they fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria. They will ask how they themselves will escape.

l: Isaiah's walking naked and barefoot, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 20
s: At the LORD's command, Isaiah loosened his sackcloth and removed his sandals, walking naked and barefoot for three years. The LORD calls it a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and Ethiopia, foreshadowing their captives being led away by Assyria in the same state.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: Chapter 21 gives three burdens. The first, the burden of the wilderness of the sea, has the speaker describing a grievous vision in which Elam is told to attack and Media's sighing is stopped, leaving him in anguish and trembling. The Lord has him set a watchman, who reports a troop of horsemen in pairs and announces that Babylon has fallen and its engraved images are broken. The second burden, of Dumah, has a voice from Seir asking the watchman about the night, and he answers that morning and night both come and tells the caller to inquire again. The third burden, on Arabia, speaks of Dedanite caravans lodging in thickets, Tema's people giving water and bread to fugitives from war, and the Lord's word that within a year all the glory of Kedar will fail and its archers will be few.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: Babylon is announced by the watchman as fallen, and all the engraved images of her gods are broken to the ground. The speaker says he has declared this as he heard it from the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: The LORD, called the LORD of Armies and the God of Israel, tells the speaker to set a watchman to declare what he sees. He is the source of the message about Babylon's fall and of the word that Kedar's glory will fail within a year.

l: Dumah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: Dumah is the subject of a burden in which one calls out of Seir asking the watchman what of the night. The watchman replies that morning comes and also night, and tells the caller to inquire again if he will inquire.

l: Arabia, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: Arabia is the subject of a burden saying the Dedanite caravans will lodge in its thickets. The people of Tema are said to have brought water to the thirsty and met fugitives with bread, as they fled swords, the bent bow and the heat of battle.

l: Kedar, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: Kedar is told, through the Lord's word to the speaker, that within a year, counted as a contract worker would count it, all its glory will fail. The remaining number of its archers and mighty men will be few, because the LORD has spoken it.

l: watchman (set by the Lord), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: The watchman is set by the Lord's command to declare what he sees and to listen with great attentiveness for troops of horsemen, donkeys and camels. He cries like a lion that he stands on the watchtower by day and at his post every night, reports a troop of horsemen in pairs, and announces Babylon's fall. In the Dumah burden a watchman answers the question from Seir about the night.

l: speaker (the prophet), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: The speaker says a grievous vision has been declared to him and describes his anguish, pain like a woman in labor, failing hearing and sight, a fluttering heart, and twilight turned into trembling. He receives the Lord's instruction to set a watchman and says he has declared what he heard from the LORD of Armies. He also relays the Lord's word about Kedar.

l: burden of the wilderness of the sea, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 21
s: This burden comes like whirlwinds in the South sweeping from the wilderness, from an awesome land. It contains the grievous vision of the treacherous man and the destroyer, the call for Elam to attack, the end of Media's sighing, and the announcement that Babylon has fallen.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: Chapter 22 is a burden against the valley of vision, a tumultuous city whose rulers fled and were captured, while the speaker weeps over the destruction of his people. The inhabitants prepared for siege by looking to the armor, gathering waters, counting and breaking down houses, and building a reservoir, but did not look to the one who planned this long ago. When GOD of Armies called for weeping and mourning, they instead feasted, saying 'let's eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die,' and were told this iniquity will not be forgiven until they die. The text then turns to the treasurer Shebna, who cut himself a tomb on high and is told he will be hurled away to a large country, die there, and be thrust from his office. Eliakim son of Hilkiah is to be called, clothed with Shebna's robe and belt, made a father to Jerusalem and Judah, and given the key of David's house, but the nail fastened in a sure place is finally said to give way and be cut down.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: GOD of Armies brings a day of confusion, treading down, and perplexity in the valley of vision, and calls for weeping and mourning, which is answered with feasting. He reveals in the speaker's ears that the people's iniquity will not be forgiven until they die. He commands the rebuke of Shebna, announces his removal, appoints Eliakim in his place, and declares that the nail fastened in a sure place will give way.

l: valley of vision, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: The valley of vision is the subject of a burden: a tumultuous, joyous city whose slain did not die by the sword and whose rulers fled and were bound by archers. It endures a day of confusion and treading down, with its walls broken down and a crying to the mountains.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: Jerusalem's houses are counted and some broken down to fortify the wall, and the breaches of David's city are seen to be many. A reservoir is made between the two walls for the water of the old pool. Eliakim is to become a father to its inhabitants.

l: Shebna, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: Shebna is the treasurer over the house who has cut himself a tomb on high, chiseled in the rock. He is told the LORD will hurl him away, wind him around and throw him like a ball into a large country where he will die, and that he is a disgrace to his lord's house. He will be thrust from his office and pulled down from his station.

l: Eliakim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, is called the LORD's servant and will be clothed with Shebna's robe and belt and given his government. He will be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the house of Judah and will carry the key of David's house, opening and shutting without anyone reversing it. He is fastened like a nail in a sure place and bears the glory of his father's house, yet that nail is finally said to give way, be cut down, and fall.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: The inhabitants shout in a joyous city while their rulers have fled. They look to armor, gather water, and break down houses for defense but do not look to the one who planned it long ago. Called to mourning, they feast instead, and are told their iniquity will not be forgiven until they die. Eliakim is to be a father to them.

l: siege preparations (Jerusalem's defense), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: The defense involves seeing the many breaches of David's city, gathering the waters of the lower pool, looking to the armor in the house of the forest, counting and breaking down houses to fortify the wall, and making a reservoir between the two walls. The text faults the people for not looking to him who had done this and planned it long ago.

l: feasting (in the day of mourning), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 22
s: On the day the Lord, GOD of Armies called for weeping, mourning, baldness, and sackcloth, the people held joy and gladness, killing cattle and sheep, eating meat and drinking wine, saying 'tomorrow we will die.' The LORD declares this iniquity will not be forgiven them until they die.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: Chapter 23 is a burden, or oracle, against Tyre, a wealthy merchant city whose trade drew on the Nile harvest and made it the market of nations. The ships of Tarshish, the coast dwellers, and Sidon are told to howl, be still, and be ashamed because Tyre is laid waste and Egypt will be in anguish at the report. The LORD of Armies is said to have planned this to stain the pride of all glory and to bring the honorable of the earth into contempt. He stretched out his hand over the sea, shook the kingdoms, and ordered the destruction of Canaan's strongholds. Tyre will be forgotten seventy years, after which the LORD will visit her and she will return to her wages, but her merchandise and earnings will become holy to the LORD, providing food and durable clothing for those who dwell before him.

l: Tyre, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: Tyre is the target of the burden: a joyous, ancient city of merchant princes, the giver of crowns, and the market of nations, laid waste so that no house or entrance remains. She will be forgotten seventy years, then be compared to a forgotten prostitute who takes up a harp and sings to be remembered. After that the LORD will visit her, she will return to her wages and trade with all the world's kingdoms, and her merchandise and earnings will be holiness to the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: The LORD of Armies is named as the one who planned the fall of Tyre, in order to stain the pride of all glory and bring the honorable of the earth into contempt. He stretched out his hand over the sea, shook the kingdoms, and ordered the destruction of Canaan's strongholds. He will later visit Tyre, and her merchandise and wages will become holy to him, supplying those who dwell before him.

l: Sidon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: Sidon is told to be ashamed because the sea, the stronghold of the sea, speaks of never having travailed or borne children. Its merchants are said to have replenished the coast dwellers. The LORD addresses its daughter as an oppressed virgin who will rejoice no more and will find no rest even if she flees to Kittim.

l: Tarshish, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: The ships of Tarshish are called on twice to howl because Tyre's stronghold is laid waste, and the coast dwellers are told to pass over to Tarshish. The daughter of Tarshish is told to pass through her land like the Nile, since there is no restraint any more.

l: seventy years of Tyre's oblivion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, according to the days of one king. At the end of that period the LORD will visit her, and she will return to her wages and trade with all the kingdoms of the world.

l: destruction of Tyre, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 23
s: Tyre is described as laid waste, with no house and no entering in, a result the LORD of Armies planned to bring contempt on the pride of glory. The report of it will cause anguish in Egypt, and the ships of Tarshish and the coast dwellers are told to howl, be still, or flee. The text sets it alongside the shaking of kingdoms, the destruction of Canaan's strongholds, and the ruin of the land of the Chaldeans by the Assyrians.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 24
s: Chapter 24 describes the LORD emptying and laying waste the earth, scattering its inhabitants because they broke the laws, statutes, and everlasting covenant. The judgment falls on all classes alike, from priest and people to master and servant, and brings a curse, mourning, and the end of mirth and wine. Cities are broken and shut up, and few people remain, like gleanings after a vintage. A remnant lifts voices in praise of the LORD's majesty from the east and the islands of the sea, while the speaker laments the treachery he sees. Fear, the pit, and the snare overtake the inhabitants, the earth is shaken and falls, and the LORD punishes the high ones on high and the kings of the earth, imprisons them, and reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem before his elders.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 24
s: The LORD empties, wastes, and turns the earth upside down, and has spoken this word of judgment.
