He punishes the army of the high ones on high and the kings of the earth, gathers them as prisoners in the pit, and will visit them after many days. As the LORD of Armies he will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem with glory before his elders, and he is glorified as the God of Israel in the east and the islands of the sea.

l: earth (the world), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 24
s: The earth is made empty and waste, mourns and fades, and is polluted under its inhabitants, who broke the everlasting covenant. A curse devours it, its foundations tremble, and it is broken, torn apart, and shaken violently. It staggers like a drunken man, sways like a hammock, and falls under the weight of its disobedience, not to rise again.

l: inhabitants of the earth, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 24
s: The inhabitants are scattered and found guilty for transgressing the laws, violating the statutes, and breaking the everlasting covenant. The judgment strikes every class alike, few are left, and fear, the pit, and the snare await them so that none escape. Joy, wine, and music end and cities fall into desolation, though a remnant shouts for the majesty of the LORD and the speaker laments the treacherous.

l: day of judgment, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 24
s: The text calls it "that day," when the LORD will punish the army of the high ones on high and the kings of the earth. They are gathered like prisoners in a pit and shut up in prison, to be visited after many days. The moon is confounded and the sun ashamed as the LORD of Armies reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: Chapter 25 is a song of praise addressed to the LORD, who is exalted for his faithful, long-planned wonders, including turning a fortified city into a ruin that will never be rebuilt. Because he has been a stronghold and refuge to the poor and needy, strong peoples and awesome nations will glorify and fear him, while the noise of strangers and the song of the dreaded ones are brought low. On this mountain the LORD of Armies will prepare a feast of choice meat and wines for all peoples, destroy the covering and veil over all nations, swallow up death forever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears and remove his people's reproach. In that day his people will declare they waited for him and rejoice in his salvation. Moab, however, will be trodden down like straw in a dunghill, its pride and craft humbled, and the high fortress of its walls brought down to the dust.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: The Lord GOD is praised as the faithful God who has done wonders planned long ago and who has been a stronghold and refuge to the poor and needy. He swallows up death forever, wipes away tears from all faces, and takes his people's reproach from the whole earth, for he has spoken it. His people say they have waited for him and will rejoice in his salvation.

l: Moab, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: Moab will be trodden down in his place, like straw trodden in the water of the dunghill, while the LORD's hand rests on the mountain. He will spread out his hands like a swimmer, but his pride will be humbled together with the craft of his hands. The high fortress of its walls is brought down to the dust.

l: the fortified city (city made a heap), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: The LORD has made a fortified city into a heap and a ruin, a palace of strangers that is no longer a city. It is said that it will never be built again.

l: holy mountain (the LORD's holy mountain), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: On this mountain the LORD of Armies will make a feast for all peoples and destroy the covering and veil spread over all nations. The LORD's hand will rest in this mountain.

l: all peoples, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: All peoples will be given a feast of choice meat and well refined choice wines by the LORD of Armies on this mountain. The covering that covers them and the veil spread over all nations will be destroyed.

l: feast, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: The LORD of Armies will make a feast for all peoples in this mountain, of choice meat full of marrow and well refined choice wines.

l: death, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 25
s: Death is said to be swallowed up forever by the Lord GOD. Along with this, tears are wiped from all faces.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: Chapter 26 presents a song to be sung in the land of Judah, celebrating a strong city whose walls are God's salvation and calling for the gates to open to the righteous nation that keeps faith. The LORD is praised as an everlasting Rock who keeps the steadfast in perfect peace, brings down the lofty city to the dust, and ordains peace for his people. The speakers, the people of Judah, say they have waited for the LORD, desire him by night, and acknowledge only his name, though they confess their suffering produced no deliverance, likened to a woman giving birth to wind. The wicked do not learn righteousness even when shown favor, and the LORD's adversaries will be consumed by fire. The chapter contrasts the dead who will not rise with the LORD's dead who will live, and ends with the people told to hide in their rooms until the indignation passes while the LORD comes out to punish the earth's inhabitants.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The LORD is called an everlasting Rock who keeps the steadfast mind in perfect peace, appoints salvation as walls and bulwarks, and brings down the lofty city. He ordains peace for his people, has done all their work for them, increased the nation and enlarged its borders, and consumes his adversaries with fire. He comes out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and his dead shall live.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The land of Judah is where the song is to be sung on that day. It is the setting for the declaration that the people have a strong city.

l: strong city (Judah's), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The strong city is the one Judah's song celebrates, with God appointing salvation as its walls and bulwarks. Its gates are to be opened so the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter.

l: righteous nation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The righteous nation is the one that keeps faith and is invited to enter through the opened gates. The way of the just is uprightness, and the path of the righteous is made level.

l: lofty city, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The lofty city is where those who dwell on high live, and the LORD brings it down, laying it low to the ground and to the dust. The feet of the poor and the steps of the needy tread it down.

l: wicked, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The wicked do not learn righteousness even when favor is shown to them. In the land of uprightness they deal wrongfully and do not see the LORD's majesty. They do not see the LORD's lifted hand, but will see his zeal for the people and be disappointed as fire consumes his adversaries.

l: speakers (the people of Judah), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The speakers say they have waited for the LORD in the way of his judgments and desire his name, seeking him by night with soul and spirit. They acknowledge that other lords ruled them but that they will acknowledge only his name. They compare their trouble to a woman in labor who gave birth only to wind, and are told to hide in their rooms with shut doors until the indignation is past.

l: the dead, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The dead of the oppressors are said not to live; their departed spirits shall not rise, and the LORD has destroyed them and caused all memory of them to perish. By contrast, the LORD's dead shall live and their bodies arise, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits. The earth will also disclose her blood and no longer cover her slain.

l: resurrection, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 26
s: The text declares that the LORD's dead shall live and their dead bodies shall arise. Those who dwell in the dust are told to awake and sing, for the LORD's dew is like the dew of herbs and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: Chapter 27 describes "that day," when the LORD will punish leviathan, the fleeing and twisted serpent, and kill the dragon in the sea. The LORD then calls for a song about his pleasant vineyard, which he keeps and waters night and day, and which he will defend against briers and thorns unless they seek peace with him. Jacob will take root and Israel will blossom, filling the world with fruit, and Jacob's iniquity will be forgiven when the altar stones are crushed like chalk and the Asherah poles and incense altars rise no more. The fortified city is left desolate, and its withered boughs are burned by women because its people have no understanding and the one who made them shows no compassion. On that day the LORD will thresh from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt, gather the children of Israel one by one, and a great trumpet will bring the perishing in Assyria and the outcasts in Egypt to worship him on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: The LORD punishes leviathan and kills the dragon in the sea with his hard, great, and strong sword. He declares himself keeper of the vineyard, saying wrath is not in him, though he would burn briers and thorns, and offers peace to anyone who takes hold of his strength. He threshes from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt, gathers Israel, and withholds compassion and favor from the people of no understanding.

l: leviathan, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: Leviathan is described as the fleeing serpent and the twisted serpent. The LORD will punish it with his sword on that day, and he will also kill the dragon that is in the sea.

l: vineyard (the LORD's vineyard), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: The vineyard is called "a pleasant vineyard," and people are told to sing to it on that day. The LORD says he keeps it, waters it every moment, and guards it night and day so that no one damages it. He would battle and burn any briers and thorns found in it, unless they take hold of his strength and make peace.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: In days to come Jacob will take root, and Israel will blossom and bud, filling the surface of the world with fruit. Jacob's iniquity will be forgiven, and the fruit of taking away his sin is that the altar stones become like beaten chalk and the Asherah poles and incense altars rise no more.

l: those ready to perish and outcasts, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: Those ready to perish in the land of Assyria and the outcasts in the land of Egypt are brought back when a great trumpet is blown. They come and worship the LORD in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

l: the day of the LORD's judgment and restoration, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: "That day" is the time when the LORD punishes leviathan and kills the dragon, and when the vineyard is sung about. It is also when he threshes from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt and gathers the children of Israel one by one. A great trumpet is blown on that day, and the perishing and outcasts come to worship at Jerusalem.

l: forgiveness of Jacob's iniquity, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 27
s: The text says Jacob's iniquity will be forgiven by this means, and that this is all the fruit of taking away his sin. The sign is that the LORD makes all the stones of the altar like chalk stones beaten in pieces, so that the Asherah poles and incense altars rise no more.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: Chapter 28 opens with a woe against the drunkards of Ephraim, whose proud crown will be trampled by a mighty one sent by the Lord, while the LORD of Armies becomes a crown of glory to his remaining people. The priest and the prophet also reel with strong drink, err in vision and stumble in judgment, and the people mock the message as childish precept on precept, so it will come to them as stammering speech that leads to their fall. The scoffers who rule in Jerusalem claim a covenant with death and shelter in lies, but the Lord says he lays in Zion a tried cornerstone and will make justice the measuring line, sweeping away their refuge and annulling the covenant. The overflowing scourge will trample them repeatedly, and the Lord will do his unusual work, with a warning not to scoff lest their bonds be strengthened. The chapter ends with a farming analogy in which the farmer plows, sows and threshes each crop appropriately, taught by God, showing that the wonderful counsel of the LORD of Armies applies measured judgment.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The LORD of Armies is said to become a crown of glory and diadem of beauty to the residue of his people, a spirit of justice to judges and strength to those at the gate. He sends a mighty one against Ephraim, rises up to do his unusual work, and has decreed destruction on the whole earth. He is described as wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The drunkards of Ephraim are the object of a woe, their crown of pride and fading flower of glorious beauty on the fertile valley being doomed. A mighty one sent by the Lord will cast them down and trample the crown, and it will be like a first-ripe fig eaten as soon as it is seen.

l: priest and prophet, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The priest and the prophet are described as reeling with wine and strong drink and being swallowed up by it. They err in vision and stumble in judgment, and the tables are full of filthy vomit.

l: scoffers who rule in Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The scoffers who rule in Jerusalem are told to hear the LORD's word and are quoted as claiming a covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol, making lies their refuge. The Lord says hail and waters will sweep away their refuge, their covenant will be annulled, and they are warned not to scoff lest their bonds be made strong.

l: cornerstone (laid in Zion), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The Lord GOD says he lays in Zion a stone, a tried stone and precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily, and justice and righteousness are made the measuring line and plumb line.

l: covenant with death, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The covenant with death, along with the agreement with Sheol, is the claim by which the rulers believe the scourge will not reach them. The Lord declares it will be annulled and will not stand.

l: overflowing scourge, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The overflowing scourge is what the scoffers believe will not come to them. The Lord says it will pass through and trample them, seizing them morning by morning, by day and by night, bringing nothing but terror to understand the message.

l: farming analogy, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 28
s: The farming analogy shows a plower who does not plow continually but levels the soil and plants dill, cumin, wheat, barley and spelt each in its place. Dill and cumin are beaten with a stick and rod, and bread flour is not ground endlessly, because God instructs the farmer in right judgment, which comes from the LORD of Armies' counsel and wisdom.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: Chapter 29 opens with a woe against Ariel, the city where David encamped, which the LORD of Armies will distress with siege, mourning, and lamentation, bringing it low until its voice whispers from the dust. Then the LORD will visit Ariel with thunder, earthquake, and fire, and the multitude of nations fighting against it will vanish like a dream. The prophets and seers are struck with a spirit of deep sleep, so that all vision is like a sealed book no one can read. The LORD condemns this people for honoring him with their lips while their hearts are far away, and promises a marvelous work in which the wisdom of their wise men perishes. The chapter ends with a reversal in which the deaf hear, the humble rejoice, oppressors are cut off, and Jacob is no longer ashamed but sanctifies the Holy One of Jacob, while the erring come to understanding.

l: Ariel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: Ariel, the city where David encamped, is the subject of a woe: the LORD will distress it, besiege it, and make it like an altar hearth with mourning and lamentation. It will be brought down and speak in a mumble from the dust, but will then be visited by the LORD of Armies with thunder, earthquake, and devouring fire, and its enemies will vanish.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD of Armies distresses Ariel and lays siege against it, then visits it with thunder, earthquake, great noise, whirlwind, storm, and devouring fire. He pours out a spirit of deep sleep on the prophets and seers, promises a marvelous work among this people, and redeems Abraham and acts for the house of Jacob.

l: nations that fight against Ariel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: The multitude of nations that fight against Ariel, her stronghold, and Mount Zion will be like fine dust and blowing chaff, vanishing in an instant. They are compared to a dream, like a hungry or thirsty man who dreams of eating or drinking and wakes still unsatisfied.

l: prophets and seers, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: The prophets and seers have their eyes closed and heads covered by the LORD, who has poured on them a spirit of deep sleep. All vision has become to them like a sealed book that neither the educated nor the uneducated can read.

l: this people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: This people draws near with their mouth and honors the LORD with their lips, but their hearts are far from him and their fear of him is a taught commandment of men. The LORD will do a marvelous work among them, and the wisdom of their wise men will perish and the understanding of their prudent men will be hidden.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 29
s: The LORD, who redeemed Abraham, says concerning the house of Jacob that Jacob will no longer be ashamed and his face will not grow pale. When he sees his children, the work of the LORD's hands, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and stand in awe of the God of Israel.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: In Chapter 30 the LORD denounces the rebellious children of Judah for seeking an alliance with Egypt and Pharaoh instead of consulting him, warning that this refuge will bring only shame and confusion. The people reject the prophets, demand pleasant deceits, and refuse the LORD's offer of salvation through returning, rest, quietness and confidence, so their iniquity will collapse like a broken wall and they will flee. Yet the LORD promises to wait and be gracious, so that the people will dwell in Zion, hear a guiding voice, discard their idols, and receive rain, abundant harvests, and healing. The chapter ends with the LORD's fiery, angry coming against the nations and the Assyrian, who will be dismayed and struck with the rod and consumed in a prepared burning place for the king.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: The LORD pronounces woe on those who take counsel and make alliances apart from him, and calls the Egyptian alliance a source of shame. He offers salvation in returning and rest, waits to be gracious, promises healing, rain and guidance, and comes in burning anger to strike the Assyrian and prepare a pyre for the king.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: Egypt is the place Judah's people go down to for refuge, and the LORD says its help is vain and to no purpose. He names her Rahab who sits still, and the shadow of Egypt is said to bring confusion to those who trust it.

l: Pharaoh, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: Pharaoh's strength is the thing the rebellious people seek to rely on. The LORD declares that it will become their shame.

l: rebellious children (Judah's people), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: They are called rebellious, lying children who take counsel and make an alliance not from the LORD, send riches to Egypt, and tell the seers and prophets to speak pleasant deceits. They refuse the offered rest and quietness, trust in horses and flight, and will flee and be left like a beacon on a mountain. Later they are promised grace, an end to weeping, a guiding voice, the casting away of their idols, plentiful provision, and healing of their wound.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: Zion at Jerusalem is where the people will dwell and weep no more. There the LORD will be gracious and answer their cry.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: The Assyrian will be dismayed at the LORD's voice and struck with his rod, with each stroke accompanied by tambourines and harps. A deep, large burning place, long prepared for the king, is kindled by the LORD's breath like a stream of sulfur.

l: alliance with Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 30
s: The alliance is portrayed as a sin added to sin, made without the LORD's Spirit or advice, with envoys at Zoan and Hanes and riches carried through dangerous lands. The LORD says it will profit nothing and bring only shame and reproach.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: Chapter 31 pronounces woe on those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses, chariots, and horsemen rather than looking to the Holy One of Israel. The LORD is described as wise and unchanging in his words, and he will rise against evildoers and those who help them, so that both helper and helped will fall. The LORD of Armies is likened to a lion undaunted by shepherds and to hovering birds, promising to fight on Mount Zion and to protect, deliver, and preserve Jerusalem. The children of Israel are called to return to him and to cast away their idols of silver and gold. The Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man, his young men will be put to forced labor, and his princes will fear the banner.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: The LORD is said to be wise, to bring disaster, and not to call back his words, and he will rise against evildoers and those who help them. He compares himself to a lion unafraid of shepherds and to hovering birds, promising to come down to fight on Mount Zion and to protect, deliver, and preserve Jerusalem. He calls Israel to return to him and declares that the Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man; his fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: Egypt is the place people go down to for help, relying on its horses, chariots, and horsemen instead of the LORD. The text warns of woe for those who do so.

l: Egyptians, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: The Egyptians are declared to be men and not God, and their horses flesh and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble and all will be consumed together with the one helped.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: Jerusalem is promised protection by the LORD of Armies, who will protect, deliver, pass over, and preserve it. It is also where the LORD's furnace is.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: The children of Israel are told to return to the one from whom they have deeply revolted. In that day everyone will cast away the idols of silver and gold their own hands made, which are called sin.
